body.statement: For every finite \(\mathcal H_0\subset[-H,H]^K\), the fixed Gaussian grid experiment is exactly embedded by vertex controls in the score diffusion, and the strict extension from the regular-payoff results of Wager and Xu and Adusumilli holds: arbitrary predictable policies, zero-allocation faces, and the discontinuous closed-test terminal loss satisfy \(\sup_{\lambda\in\Delta_M}|B_n(\lambda)-B(\lambda)|\to0\), \(c_{n,m}\to c_m\) for every \(m\), and \(V_n\to V\). Moreover, for each \(\epsilon>0\) there are predictable finite-horizon policies whose scenario-risk vectors converge coordinatewise to that of an \(\epsilon\)-optimal diffusion control.
body.justification: It identifies the attainable local-power regret frontier for the fixed confirmatory test on every finite bounded scenario list and transfers a near-optimal diffusion risk vector to predictable finite-stage recruitment.
body.gap: The regular-payoff diffusion results of Wager and Xu and Adusumilli do not themselves handle this discontinuous closure payoff. The theorem supplies the boundary-stable envelope transfer while allowing zero-allocation faces; the corrected likelihood argument controls adaptive clocks by stochastic-exponential factorization rather than an invalid independence equality.
body.consumer: It converts a continuum recruitment solution into asymptotically equivalent finite-stage policies for interAdapt-style subgroup-enrichment designs.
body.proof_tex:
Fix an arbitrary finite scenario list
\(\mathcal H_0=\{h^1,\ldots,h^M\}\subset[-H,H]^K\).  Only finiteness and
\(|h_j^m|\leq H\) are used below.

\emph{Exact embedding.}
Fix \(n\) and \(\pi_n\in\Pi_n\).  On
\(((i-1)/n,i/n]\), define the vertex control
\[
 u_j(t)=\mathbf 1\{A_i=j\}.
\tag{1}
\]
The randomization producing \(A_i\) is made at the left endpoint from
\(\mathcal F_{i-1}\).  Thus (1) is predictable by
\(\mathrm{ass{:}finite\mbox{-}predictability}\), and it is an element of
\(\mathcal U\) by
\(\mathrm{ass{:}continuous\mbox{-}observed\mbox{-}control}\) and
\(\mathrm{def{:}continuous\mbox{-}control\mbox{-}class}\).  Conditional on
the past and \(A_i=j\), the diffusion increments are
\[
 \Delta X_j=\frac{h_j^m}{n}
 +W_j(i/n)-W_j((i-1)/n)
 \sim\mathcal N\!\left(\frac{h_j^m}{n},\frac1n\right),
 \qquad \Delta Q_j=\frac1n,
\tag{2}
\]
and all other coordinates have zero increments.  By
\(\mathrm{ass{:}gaussian\mbox{-}known\mbox{-}variance}\) and
\(\mathrm{ass{:}local\mbox{-}scenario\mbox{-}scaling}\),
\(Y_i/\sqrt n\), conditional on the same history and action, has the score
law in (2).  Induction over \(i\) proves equality of the complete observed
score--clock laws under every scenario \(m\).  Consequently every finite
policy is embedded exactly as a vertex-control diffusion policy, with the
same scenario-risk vector.

\emph{Continuous-payoff approximation.}
Let \(g_m:\mathbb R^K\times[0,1]^K\to[0,1]\) be continuous, for
\(m=1,\ldots,M\).  We first prove that its prior-weighted value over
\(n\)-grid vertex controls converges to its value over \(\mathcal U\).
On the canonical observed space, a progressively measurable
\(\Delta(\mathcal J)\)-valued control \(u\) can be approximated by simple
predictable controls \(u^{(r)}\): approximate bounded predictable
coordinates by simple predictable functions and project their vectors onto
the closed simplex.  Bounded convergence in measure then gives
\[
 \mathbb E_0\int_0^1\sum_j
 |u_j^{(r)}(t)-u_j(t)|\,dt\longrightarrow0.
\tag{3}
\]
The elementary inequality
\((\sqrt a-\sqrt b)^2\leq |a-b|\), for \(a,b\geq0\), and Itô isometry show
from (3) that the martingale parts of the score vectors converge in
\(L^2(\mathbb P_0)\); the clock vectors converge in \(L^1(\mathbb P_0)\).
Since \(|h_j^m|\leq H\), the drift terms converge in \(L^1\) under every
scenario as well.

For a fixed simple control, subdivide each of its finitely many time cells
into \(n\)-grid cells.  At the left endpoint of a grid cell, choose vertex
\(j\) with the simplex probabilities prescribed by the simple control.
For each time cell, the sum of the conditional variances of the normalized
centered allocation counts is at most the reciprocal of the number of grid
cells, and hence tends to zero.  Conditional on those counts, the coordinate
score increment has mean \(h_j^m\Delta Q_j\) and variance \(\Delta Q_j\);
its characteristic function is
\[
 \exp\!\left\{\mathrm i z_jh_j^m\Delta Q_j
 -\frac12z_j^2\Delta Q_j\right\}.
\tag{4}
\]
At the finitely many decision times, each past-measurable action kernel can
be replaced by one continuous outside a set of arbitrarily small
\(\mathbb P_0\)-probability: on the finite-dimensional Gaussian history
space, approximate its bounded coordinate functions by continuous functions
off a small Borel set and project back onto the simplex.  A union bound over
the finitely many cells controls the probability that the replacement
changes any action.  Induction over the cells can therefore apply (4) at
continuity points.  Letting the exceptional probability vanish, and then
using the approximation in (3), yields a diagonal sequence of predictable
grid policies \(\pi_n[u]\) for which
\[
 (X_n,Q_n)\Longrightarrow(X^u(1),Q^u(1))
 \quad\text{under the zero-drift reference law}.
\tag{5}
\]
The vertex randomization allows a simplex coordinate to equal zero; no
positive allocation lower bound has been introduced.

We now transfer (5) to every declared scenario without treating the adaptive
clock as independent of the score.  Under the zero-drift reference law put
\[
 M_m(t)=\sum_jh_j^m\int_0^t\sqrt{u_j(s)}\,dW_j(s),
 \qquad
 A_m(t)=\langle M_m\rangle_t
 =\sum_j(h_j^m)^2Q_j(t).
\tag{6}
\]
Because \(\sum_jQ_j(1)=1\) and \(|h_j^m|\leq H\),
\[
 0\leq A_m(1)\leq H^2.
\tag{7}
\]
The likelihood ratio from the zero-drift law to scenario \(m\) is
\[
 Z_m(X(1),Q(1))
 =\exp\{M_m(1)-\tfrac12A_m(1)\}.
\tag{8}
\]
Its square factors pathwise as
\[
 Z_m(X(1),Q(1))^2
 =\underbrace{\exp\{2M_m(1)-2A_m(1)\}}_
 {\mathcal E(2M_m)_1}\exp\{A_m(1)\}.
\tag{9}
\]
This is a factorization, not an independence assertion.  Moreover,
\[
 \frac12\langle2M_m\rangle_1=2A_m(1)\leq2H^2.
\tag{10}
\]
We verify the needed mean-one property rather than assume it.  If the
integrand of \(2M_m\) is simple predictable, successive conditioning uses
\[
 \mathbb E\!\left[
 e^{\beta\Delta W-\beta^2\Delta t/2}\mid\mathcal F_{\mathrm{left}}
 \right]=1
\]
for every past-measurable \(\beta\), and hence
\(\mathbb E_0\mathcal E(2M_m)_1=1\).  For a general progressively
measurable control, approximate the bounded integrand in
\(L^2(dt\,d\mathbb P_0)\) by simple predictable integrands.  The stochastic
integrals and brackets then converge in probability.  For every simple
approximant \(R\) with energy at most \(4H^2\), the same factorization and
conditional-Gaussian calculation at the doubled integrand give
\[
 \mathbb E_0[\mathcal E(R)_1^2]
 =\mathbb E_0[\mathcal E(2R)_1e^{\langle R\rangle_1}]
 \leq e^{4H^2}.
\]
Thus these exponentials are uniformly integrable, so passage to the limit
preserves their mean one.  Combining this bounded-energy conclusion with
the pointwise bound (7) in (9) gives the corrected estimate
\[
 \mathbb E_0[Z_m(X(1),Q(1))^2]
 \leq e^{H^2}\mathbb E_0\mathcal E(2M_m)_1
 =e^{H^2}.
\tag{11}
\]
The same calculation holds for grid vertex controls: the corresponding
piecewise-constant stochastic integral has bracket
\(\sum_j(h_j^m)^2Q_{j,n}\leq H^2\).  Thus the family of likelihood ratios
for the approximating controls is uniformly integrable.  Since
\[
 Z_m(x,q)=
 \exp\!\left\{\sum_jh_j^mx_j-\frac12
 \sum_j(h_j^m)^2q_j\right\}
\tag{12}
\]
is continuous, truncation of \(Z_m\), (5), and the uniform \(L^2\) bound
(11) imply
\[
 \mathbb E_m^{\pi_n[u]}g_m(X_n,Q_n)
 =\mathbb E_0^{\pi_n[u]}[Z_m(X_n,Q_n)g_m(X_n,Q_n)]
 \longrightarrow
 \mathbb E_0^u[Z_m(X(1),Q(1))g_m(X(1),Q(1))]
 =\mathbb E_m^ug_m(X(1),Q(1)).
\tag{13}
\]
Because \(M\) is finite, the convergence holds simultaneously for all
scenarios.

Let \(G_n(\lambda)\) and \(G(\lambda)\) denote the infimal
prior-weighted risks for the continuous payoffs \(g_m\), over
\(\Pi_n\) and \(\mathcal U\), respectively.  Exact embedding gives
\(G(\lambda)\leq G_n(\lambda)\) for every \(n\).  Conversely, choose a
control within an arbitrary positive tolerance of \(G(\lambda)\) and apply
(13); hence \(\limsup_nG_n(\lambda)\leq G(\lambda)\).  Therefore
\[
 G_n(\lambda)\longrightarrow G(\lambda).
\tag{14}
\]

For fixed \(\delta>0\), the envelope losses specified in
\(\mathrm{def{:}terminal\mbox{-}envelopes}\) are bounded and continuous:
exponentiation, finite arithmetic means, finite minima, and
\(f_\delta^\pm\) are continuous.  Equation (14) gives
\[
 B_{n,\delta}^{\pm}(\lambda)
 \longrightarrow B_\delta^{\pm}(\lambda).
\tag{15}
\]
For either sign and either experiment, the value is
\(1\)-Lipschitz in \(\lambda\) under the \(\ell_1\) norm, since every
scenario loss lies in \([0,1]\).  A finite \(\ell_1\)-net of compact
\(\Delta_M\), followed by the two Lipschitz inequalities, upgrades (15) to
\[
 \sup_{\lambda\in\Delta_M}
 |B_{n,\delta}^{\pm}(\lambda)-B_\delta^{\pm}(\lambda)|
 \longrightarrow0.
\tag{16}
\]

\emph{Removal of the envelopes.}
The pointwise scalar inequalities
\(f_\delta^-\leq\mathbf1\{\,\cdot<0\,\}\leq f_\delta^+\) and
\(\mathrm{lem{:}quantitative\mbox{-}terminal\mbox{-}comparison}\) give
\[
 B_{n,\delta}^-(\lambda)\leq B_n(\lambda)\leq
 B_{n,\delta}^+(\lambda),\qquad
 B_\delta^-(\lambda)\leq B(\lambda)\leq
 B_\delta^+(\lambda),
\tag{17}
\]
and bound each upper-minus-lower width by
\(\rho_{H,K}(\delta,\eta)\), uniformly in \(n\) and \(\lambda\).
Combining (16)--(17), with \(\eta=\sqrt\delta\), yields
\[
 \limsup_{n\to\infty}\sup_{\lambda\in\Delta_M}
 |B_n(\lambda)-B(\lambda)|
 \leq \rho_{H,K}(\delta,\sqrt\delta).
\tag{18}
\]
The last assertion of
\(\mathrm{lem{:}quantitative\mbox{-}terminal\mbox{-}comparison}\) permits
\(\delta\downarrow0\), and therefore
\[
 \sup_{\lambda\in\Delta_M}|B_n(\lambda)-B(\lambda)|
 \longrightarrow0.
\tag{19}
\]
For the point-mass prior \(e_m\), the definitions give
\(B_n(e_m)=c_{n,m}\) and \(B(e_m)=c_m\).  Consequently
\[
 \max_{1\leq m\leq M}|c_{n,m}-c_m|\longrightarrow0.
\tag{20}
\]

It remains to transfer the minimax regret.  Let \(C_n\) be the closure in
\([0,1]^M\) of the achievable finite-experiment regret vectors.  Exogenous
randomization at time zero makes \(C_n\) convex, and it is compact by
closure in the compact cube.  If
\(v_n=\min_{r\in C_n}\max_mr_m\), then the upward-closed convex set
\(D_n=C_n+\mathbb R_+^M\) contains \(v_n\mathbf1\), while
\((v_n-a)\mathbf1\notin D_n\) for \(a>0\).  To construct a supporting
normal directly, let \(y_k=(v_n-k^{-1})\mathbf1\) and let \(d_k\) minimize
\(\|y_k-d\|_2\) over \(d\in D_n\).  Existence follows by restricting the
closed set to the compact ball centered at \(y_k\) with radius
\(\|y_k-v_n\mathbf1\|_2+1\).  Convexity and minimality, applied to
\(d_k+s(d-d_k)\) and differentiated at \(s=0+\), give
\[
 (d_k-y_k)^\top(d-d_k)\geq0
 \quad(d\in D_n).
\]
Put \(\lambda_k=(d_k-y_k)/\|d_k-y_k\|_1\).  Since
\(D_n+\mathbb R_+^M=D_n\), substituting \(d=d_k+ae_j\) shows
\((\lambda_k)_j\geq0\); hence \(\lambda_k\in\Delta_M\).
Along a convergent subsequence, \(\lambda_k\to\lambda_n\in\Delta_M\).
Moreover \(d_k\to v_n\mathbf1\), because \(v_n\mathbf1\in D_n\) and
\(\|d_k-y_k\|_2\leq\|v_n\mathbf1-y_k\|_2=\sqrt M/k\).
Passing to the limit in the projection inequality gives
\(\lambda_n^\top(d-v_n\mathbf1)\geq0\) for all \(d\in D_n\).  Thus
\[
 \inf_{r\in C_n}\max_mr_m
 =\max_{\lambda\in\Delta_M}\inf_{r\in C_n}\lambda^\top r.
\tag{21}
\]
Indeed, support gives the inequality from right to left, while
\(\lambda^\top r\leq\max_mr_m\) gives the reverse inequality.  Translating
regret vectors by the oracle vector yields
\[
 V_n=\max_{\lambda\in\Delta_M}
 \left\{B_n(\lambda)-\sum_m\lambda_mc_{n,m}\right\}.
\tag{22}
\]
The same finite-dimensional argument for diffusion risks gives
\[
 V=\max_{\lambda\in\Delta_M}
 \left\{B(\lambda)-\sum_m\lambda_mc_m\right\}.
\tag{23}
\]
It follows from (19)--(23) that
\[
 |V_n-V|
 \leq
 \sup_{\lambda\in\Delta_M}|B_n(\lambda)-B(\lambda)|
 +\max_m|c_{n,m}-c_m|
 \longrightarrow0.
\tag{24}
\]

\emph{Predictable policy attainment.}
Fix \(\epsilon>0\).  By (20) and (24), choose \(N\) sufficiently large
that
\[
 |V_N-V|+\max_m|c_{N,m}-c_m|<\epsilon/3.
\tag{25}
\]
Choose \(\pi_N\in\Pi_N\) with
\[
 \max_m\{L_N(\pi_N,m)-c_{N,m}\}\leq V_N+\epsilon/3.
\tag{26}
\]
Embed \(\pi_N\) as the \(N\)-block vertex control \(u^\epsilon\) from
(1).  Exact equality of its scenario-risk vector and (25)--(26) gives
\[
 \max_m r_m(u^\epsilon)\leq V+\epsilon.
\tag{27}
\]
Thus \(u^\epsilon\) is an \(\epsilon\)-optimal diffusion control.

We finally approximate this particular control for the original
discontinuous loss.  Conditional on the exogenous randomization and on any
action sequence having positive conditional probability, the sampled
Gaussian block increments are absolutely continuous on their sampled
coordinate subspace.  A terminal threshold equality is a zero set of
\[
 \sum_{j\in I}\exp(X_j-Q_j/2)-20|I|.
\tag{28}
\]
If at least one coordinate \(j_0\in I\) was sampled, condition on all
sampled Gaussian coordinates except \(X_{j_0}\).  Equation (28) then has
at most one solution for \(X_{j_0}\), because
\(\exp(X_{j_0}-Q_{j_0}/2)\) is strictly increasing; the conditional law of
\(X_{j_0}\) has a density, so the conditional probability of equality is
zero.  Fubini's identity makes the unconditional probability zero.  If none
was sampled, its left side is
\(|I|-20|I|\neq0\).  There are finitely many \(I\), so
\[
 \Pr_m^{u^\epsilon}\{a_j(X(1),Q(1))=0
 \text{ for some }j\}=0
\quad\text{for every }m.
\tag{29}
\]

For horizon \(n\), divide enrollment into \(N\) consecutive blocks whose
lengths differ from \(n/N\) by at most one, keep the subgroup selected by
\(\pi_N\) throughout each block, and supply its normalized Gaussian block
aggregate to the next decision kernel.  This rule is predictable by
\(\mathrm{ass{:}finite\mbox{-}predictability}\).  The block clock lengths
converge to \(1/N\), and the aggregates have their exact Gaussian laws;
induction over the fixed number \(N\) of blocks gives terminal-state
convergence to \(u^\epsilon\).  Measurable decision kernels can first be
modified on sets of arbitrarily small probability, simultaneously under
the finite family of Gaussian history laws, so that the induction is
performed at continuity points.  By (29), for each \(a>0\) there is an open
neighborhood of the finitely many threshold surfaces whose probability is
below \(a\).  Off that neighborhood the terminal loss is continuous, while
its absolute value is at most one.  Weak convergence on the closed
complement, followed by an error of at most \(2a\) and then
\(a\downarrow0\), gives predictable policies
\(\pi_n^\epsilon\) satisfying
\[
 L_n(\pi_n^\epsilon,m)\longrightarrow L(u^\epsilon,m)
 \quad\text{for every }m.
\tag{30}
\]
Equations (27) and (30) prove the asserted risk-vector transfer.  The
construction allows zero block allocations.  Every step used only the
declared finite list and \(|h_j^m|\leq H\); null-boundary closure was not
used.
